questions.text: In the multi-store model of memory, which store does information from the senses enter first?

feedback: Information only reaches short-term memory after attention in the first store
Working memory is a different model (Baddeley and Hitch), not part of the multi-store model

questions.solution: In the multi-store model, information from the senses enters sensory memory first. If we pay attention to it, it passes to short-term memory
questions.hint: Think about what happens to sights and sounds before you pay attention to them

questions.text: In the multi-store model, which process moves information from short-term memory into long-term memory? Give the term.

feedback.retrieval: Retrieval brings information back OUT of long-term memory — the question asks how it gets in

questions.solution: Rehearsal (repeating information) transfers it from short-term memory to long-term memory
questions.hint: It means going over the information again and again

questions.text: Which psychologist carried out the 'War of the Ghosts' study of reconstructive memory? Give the surname.
questions.solution: Frederic Bartlett (1932) asked British participants to recall a Native American folk tale called 'The War of the Ghosts'
questions.hint: He was a British psychologist working at Cambridge in the 1930s

questions.text: What is perception?

options: Detecting light and sound with the sense organs
Making sense of the information picked up by the senses
Storing information for a long time
Repeating information so it is remembered
feedback: That is sensation — perception is what the brain does with the information next

questions.solution: Sensation is detecting stimuli with the sense organs; perception is the brain interpreting that information
questions.hint: Compare it with sensation, which is just detecting a stimulus

questions.text: What name is given to depth cues that need only one eye to work? Give the term.
questions.solution: Monocular depth cues (such as relative size, occlusion, height in plane and linear perspective) work with one eye
questions.hint: 'Mono' means one

questions.text: Who developed the multi-store model of memory?

feedback: Baddeley and Hitch developed the working memory model
Loftus and Palmer studied leading questions and eyewitness memory
Bruner and Minturn studied perceptual set

questions.solution: Atkinson and Shiffrin proposed the multi-store model in 1968
questions.hint: Their model was published in 1968

questions.text: According to the multi-store model, what is the approximate capacity of short-term memory?

feedback: Long-term memory is the store thought to have unlimited capacity

questions.solution: Short-term memory holds about 7 ± 2 items (Miller), while long-term memory is thought to be unlimited
questions.hint: Think of the length of a phone number you can just about hold in your head

questions.text: According to the multi-store model, how is information mainly encoded in long-term memory?

options: It is not encoded at all
feedback: Acoustic coding is mainly linked to short-term memory

questions.solution: Long-term memory mainly encodes semantically (by meaning); short-term memory mainly encodes acoustically
questions.hint: Think about what you remember about a conversation from last week: the exact sounds, or what it was about?

questions.text: Which type of long-term memory holds knowledge of how to do things, such as riding a bike?

feedback: Episodic memory stores personal events
Semantic memory stores facts and knowledge

questions.solution: Procedural memory stores skills and actions, which we can often do without thinking about them
questions.hint: This type of memory is about skills and actions

questions.text: What is the name for the finding that the first few words in a list are recalled better than words in the middle? Give the term.

feedback.recency effect: The recency effect is about the LAST words in a list
feedback.recency: The recency effect is about the LAST words in a list
feedback.serial position effect: That's the name for the whole curve — give the effect for the START of the list

questions.solution: The primacy effect: the first words are rehearsed more, so they pass into long-term memory
questions.hint: It comes from a word meaning 'first'

questions.text: Which of these is a binocular depth cue?

feedback: Height in plane works with one eye, so it is monocular
Occlusion works with one eye, so it is monocular
Linear perspective works with one eye, so it is monocular

questions.solution: Retinal disparity (each eye sees a slightly different image) needs two eyes; the others are monocular cues
questions.hint: Binocular cues need two eyes working together

questions.text: Gibson's theory says perception comes directly from the information in what we see, without needing past experience. Is Gibson's theory 'top-down' or 'bottom-up'? Type one of these.

feedback.top-down: Top-down processing uses past experience — that is Gregory's view, not Gibson's
feedback.top down: Top-down processing uses past experience — that is Gregory's view, not Gibson's

questions.solution: Gibson's direct theory is bottom-up: perception is built from the sensory information itself. Gregory's theory is top-down
questions.hint: Top-down processing uses knowledge and experience; which does Gibson say we don't need?

questions.text: Priya is shown a list of 20 words and asked to recall them straight away, in any order. Which words is she most likely to recall best?

options: Words from the middle of the list
Only words from the middle and the end
Every word equally, whatever its position
Words from the start and the end of the list
feedback: Middle words are usually recalled worst

questions.solution: The serial position effect: the first words (primacy) and the last words (recency) are recalled best
questions.hint: Think about the shape of the serial position curve

questions.text: In a picture, a house is drawn partly hidden behind a tree, so the house looks further away. Which depth cue is this?

feedback: Retinal disparity needs two eyes looking at a real scene, not a picture

questions.solution: Occlusion (superimposition): an object partly covered by another is seen as further away
questions.hint: One object is blocking part of the other

questions.text: Participants were shown a series of letters, then an ambiguous figure that could be read as the letter 'B' or the number '13'. Most saw it as 'B'. Which factor affecting perception does this show?

feedback: Motivation is about needs such as hunger

questions.solution: This is perceptual set caused by expectation: after seeing letters, people expected another letter (Bruner and Minturn)
questions.hint: What were the participants ready to see after a run of letters?

questions.text: Hungry participants rated pictures of food as brighter than participants who had just eaten. Which factor affecting perception does this show?

feedback: Convergence is a binocular depth cue, not a factor in perceptual set

questions.solution: Motivation (here, hunger) affected perception — Gilchrist and Nesberg found this perceptual set effect
questions.hint: Think about what hunger does to what we pay attention to

questions.text: After reading a folk tale from another culture, Sam retells it. He leaves out parts that seem strange to him and changes details to fit his own culture. What type of memory does this show? Give the term.
questions.solution: Reconstructive memory: we rebuild memories using our schemas, so details change to fit what we expect (Bartlett)
questions.hint: Memories are rebuilt each time we recall them, rather than replayed like a recording

questions.text: Divers learned words underwater and recalled more of them when tested underwater than on land. This shows that recall is better when the setting matches the learning setting. Complete the term: '______-dependent memory'. Type the missing word.

feedback.state: State-dependent memory is about your internal state (such as mood), not the place
feedback.state-dependent: State-dependent memory is about your internal state (such as mood), not the place

questions.solution: Context-dependent memory: the environment at learning acts as a cue at recall (Godden and Baddeley)
questions.hint: The missing word means the setting or surroundings

questions.text: In a free recall study, words in positions 1–3 of a 20-word list were recalled by 70% of participants, words in positions 8–12 by 25%, and words in positions 18–20 by 80%. Which conclusion matches these results?

options: Only a primacy effect was found
Only a recency effect was found
Position in the list made no difference
Both a primacy effect and a recency effect were found
feedback: Recall at the end (80%) was also high, so there was a recency effect too

questions.solution: Recall was high at the start (70%, primacy) and at the end (80%, recency) but low in the middle (25%)
questions.hint: Compare the start and the end of the list with the middle

questions.text: A man with severe amnesia cannot remember what happened earlier in the day, but he can still play the piano well. Which type of long-term memory is shown to be working in this example?

feedback: Remembering events of the day is episodic memory, which is the part that is damaged here

questions.solution: Playing the piano is a skill stored in procedural memory, which can survive damage that destroys episodic memory
questions.hint: Which type of memory stores skills?

questions.text: In the Ponzo illusion, two identical lines are drawn between two lines that come together like railway tracks. The upper line looks longer. How does Gregory's theory explain this?

options: The figure is ambiguous, so it flips between two different shapes
The brain reads the converging lines as a depth cue, so the upper line is seen as further away and therefore bigger
The brain fills in a shape that is not actually there
Each eye receives a different image of the two lines
feedback: Ambiguity explains figures such as the Necker cube
Seeing something that is not there is 'fiction', as in the Kanizsa triangle

questions.solution: The converging lines act like linear perspective; the brain assumes the upper line is further away and scales it up (misinterpreted depth cues)
questions.hint: Think of railway tracks meeting in the distance

questions.text: Gregory explained the Müller-Lyer illusion by saying the line with outward-spreading fins looks like the inside corner of a room. Why does this make that line look longer?

options: It is seen as nearer, so the brain scales it down
Each eye sees a different line
It is seen as further away, so the brain scales it up
The fins hide part of the line
feedback: Nearer objects are scaled down — that explains why the other line looks shorter

questions.solution: An inside corner is further away; using size constancy, the brain enlarges a line it thinks is distant, so it looks longer
questions.hint: Think about size constancy: how does the brain treat things it thinks are far away?

questions.text: A photo shows two people of similar height. One looks much smaller in the image, so we judge that person to be further away. Which monocular depth cue is this? Give the term.

feedback.size constancy: Size constancy is knowing an object stays the same size — the cue for distance here is the difference in image size

questions.solution: Relative size: when objects are expected to be similar in size, the one that looks smaller is judged to be further away
questions.hint: The cue compares how big the two people look

questions.text: Describe the multi-store model of memory.

rubric.model_answer: Information from the senses enters sensory memory, which holds a lot of information for a very short time. If we pay attention to it, it passes to short-term memory, which has a capacity of about 7 items, lasts up to about 30 seconds without rehearsal and mainly codes acoustically. If it is rehearsed, it is transferred to long-term memory, which has a very large capacity, can last a lifetime and mainly codes semantically. Information is retrieved from long-term memory back into short-term memory when needed. Information that is not attended to or rehearsed is lost.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: information enters sensory memory first and is held very briefly
1 mark: attention passes it to short-term memory
1 mark: a correct feature of short-term memory (capacity about 7 items, short duration or acoustic coding)
1 mark: rehearsal transfers it to long-term memory, which has a large capacity and lasts a long time
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Sensory memory → (attention) → short-term memory → (rehearsal) → long-term memory, with retrieval back to short-term memory
questions.hint: Start with the three stores and the processes that move information between them

questions.text: Which statement about the multi-store model is accurate?

options: Long-term memory has a capacity of about 7 items
Information goes straight from sensory memory into long-term memory
Short-term memory lasts for several days
Information that is not paid attention to in sensory memory is quickly lost
feedback: About 7 items is the capacity of short-term memory
Information has to pass through short-term memory first

questions.solution: Without attention, information in sensory memory decays almost at once; attention moves it to short-term memory
questions.hint: Check each statement against the order of the stores and their features

questions.text: A critic argues: 'If perception were direct, we would not be fooled by visual illusions.' Which theory does this criticism support?

feedback: The criticism is aimed AT Gibson's direct theory
Bartlett's theory is about memory, not perception

questions.solution: Illusions suggest the brain makes wrong guesses using past experience, which supports Gregory's top-down theory over Gibson's
questions.hint: Which theory says perception involves the brain making a best guess?

questions.text: In a serial position study, why are the first words in a list often recalled well, according to the multi-store model?

options: They are still in short-term memory when recall begins
They were rehearsed more, so they passed into long-term memory
They are stored in sensory memory for longer
They are always the most interesting words
feedback: Being in short-term memory at recall explains the recency effect (the last words)

questions.solution: The first words get the most rehearsal, so they are transferred to long-term memory: this explains the primacy effect
questions.hint: How does information get into long-term memory in this model?

questions.text: Which is a weakness of Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study?

options: It used participants from many different cultures
It was a laboratory study with very strict controls
Participants were not given standardised instructions, so the procedure was poorly controlled
It used brain scans to measure memory
feedback: Strict controls would be a strength, and Bartlett's study was not strictly controlled

questions.solution: Bartlett's procedure was informal: participants were not told to be accurate and instructions were not standardised
questions.hint: Think about how carefully the procedure was controlled

questions.text: Learning a new phone number makes it harder to remember your old one. What is the name for this type of interference? Give the term.

feedback.proactive interference: Proactive interference is when OLD learning disrupts NEW learning
feedback.proactive: Proactive interference is when OLD learning disrupts NEW learning

questions.solution: Retroactive interference: new learning disrupts the recall of older information
questions.hint: 'Retro' means backwards: new learning works backwards on old memories

questions.text: Explain how Gregory's constructivist theory explains visual illusions. Use one example in your answer.

rubric.model_answer: Gregory said perception is top-down: the brain uses past experience to make a 'best guess' (hypothesis) about what the senses detect. Usually this works, but illusions happen when the brain applies a rule that does not fit. In the Müller-Lyer illusion, the line with outward-spreading fins looks like the inside corner of a room, so the brain treats it as further away. Using size constancy, it scales the line up, so it looks longer than the other line, even though both are the same length.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: perception is top-down / uses past experience
1 mark: the brain makes an inference or hypothesis about sensory data
1 mark: illusions occur when the wrong hypothesis is applied
1 mark: a named example (e.g. Müller-Lyer, Ponzo)
2 marks: a clear explanation of how the example fools the brain (e.g. depth cues and size constancy)
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Gregory: perception is top-down guessing from past experience; illusions are wrong guesses, e.g. Müller-Lyer lines read as near and far corners
questions.hint: Start with what 'top-down' means, then choose one illusion you can describe

questions.text: According to Piaget, what is the first stage of cognitive development, from birth to about 2 years?
questions.solution: Piaget's stages: sensorimotor (0–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (11+)
questions.hint: Babies learn about the world through their senses and movements

questions.text: What name did Piaget give to a mental structure that holds our knowledge about something, such as 'dogs'? Give the term.
questions.solution: A schema is a mental structure of knowledge about an object or idea; schemas grow and change as we learn
questions.hint: It is a mental 'file' of knowledge

questions.text: Which part of the brain is one of the first to develop in the foetus and controls basic automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate? Give the term.
questions.solution: The brainstem develops early in the foetus and controls automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate and swallowing
questions.hint: It sits at the base of the brain, connecting it to the spinal cord

questions.text: Which part of the nervous system is made up of the brain and the spinal cord?

feedback: The peripheral nervous system is all the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord

questions.solution: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system connects it to the rest of the body
questions.hint: Think 'central': it is in the middle of everything

questions.text: Which lobe of the brain contains the visual area? Give the name of the lobe.

feedback.temporal lobe: The temporal lobe contains the auditory area (hearing)
feedback.temporal: The temporal lobe contains the auditory area (hearing)
feedback.parietal lobe: The parietal lobe processes touch (the somatosensory area)
feedback.parietal: The parietal lobe processes touch (the somatosensory area)

questions.solution: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the visual area
questions.hint: It is at the back of the brain

questions.text: In Dweck's mindset theory, what is a growth mindset?

options: Believing that intelligence is fixed at birth
Believing that you must be taught in your preferred learning style
Believing that ability can be developed through effort and practice
Believing that the brain stops changing after age 7
feedback: That describes a fixed mindset

questions.solution: A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can improve with effort; a fixed mindset is the belief that they cannot
questions.hint: The word 'growth' is the clue: can ability change?

questions.text: Which of these lists Piaget's stages in the correct order?

options: Pre-operational, sensorimotor, concrete operational, formal operational
Sensorimotor, concrete operational, pre-operational, formal operational
Sensorimotor, pre-operational, formal operational, concrete operational
Sensorimotor, pre-operational, concrete operational, formal operational

questions.solution: Sensorimotor (0–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (11+)
questions.hint: Babies come first; abstract thinking comes last

questions.text: Which statement describes accommodation in Piaget's theory?

options: Changing an existing schema, or making a new one, to fit new information
Fitting new information into an existing schema without changing it
Feeling balanced because new information fits what you already know
Repeating information so that it is stored
feedback: That is assimilation
That is equilibrium

questions.solution: Accommodation changes schemas to fit new information; assimilation fits new information into existing schemas
questions.hint: Accommodation is the process that changes the schema itself

questions.text: In Piaget's theory, what is the name for understanding that an amount stays the same even when its appearance changes, such as water poured into a taller glass? Give the term.
questions.solution: Conservation is the understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in appearance; Piaget said it develops at about age 7
questions.hint: Children in the pre-operational stage think the taller glass holds more

questions.text: Which type of neuron carries messages from the central nervous system to muscles?

feedback: Sensory neurons carry messages TO the central nervous system
Relay neurons connect neurons inside the central nervous system

questions.solution: Motor neurons carry messages from the CNS to effectors such as muscles; sensory neurons carry messages to the CNS
questions.hint: Which neuron makes something move?

questions.text: Which part of the autonomic nervous system produces the 'fight or flight' response?

feedback: The parasympathetic system returns the body to a calm, resting state

questions.solution: The sympathetic branch raises heart rate and prepares the body for action; the parasympathetic branch calms the body ('rest and digest')
questions.hint: One branch speeds the body up; the other calms it down

questions.text: What is the name of the tiny gap between two neurons, into which neurotransmitters are released? Give the term.
questions.solution: Neurotransmitters are released into the synapse (synaptic gap) and bind to receptors on the next neuron
questions.hint: Chemical messengers cross this gap to pass on the signal

questions.text: A 4-year-old is shown two equal rows of 6 counters. When one row is spread out, she says it has more counters. According to Piaget, which stage is she in?

feedback: Children in the concrete operational stage CAN conserve

questions.solution: She cannot yet conserve number, which Piaget said is typical of the pre-operational stage (2–7 years)
questions.hint: Which stage comes before children can conserve?

questions.text: A baby keeps looking for a toy after it has been hidden under a blanket. According to Piaget, what has the baby developed?
questions.solution: Object permanence is knowing an object still exists when it is out of sight; Piaget said it develops in the sensorimotor stage
questions.hint: The baby knows the toy still exists even though it cannot see it

questions.text: A child has a schema for 'dog'. She sees a cat for the first time and calls it a dog. Which process is this?

feedback: Accommodation would mean changing her schema, for example making a new one for cats

questions.solution: She fits the new animal into her existing 'dog' schema without changing it: assimilation
questions.hint: Is she changing her schema, or fitting the cat into the schema she already has?

questions.text: After a stroke, a patient understands what people say but has great difficulty producing speech. Which area of the brain is most likely to be damaged?

feedback: Damage to Wernicke's area mainly affects understanding language

questions.solution: Broca's area, in the frontal lobe (usually the left), is linked to speech production
questions.hint: One language area is for producing speech and one is for understanding it

questions.text: A teacher praises a student: 'You worked really hard on this.' According to Dweck, praising effort like this encourages which mindset? Give the term.

feedback.fixed mindset: Praising talent ('you're so clever') is linked to a fixed mindset — this praise is about effort
feedback.fixed: Praising talent ('you're so clever') is linked to a fixed mindset — this praise is about effort

questions.solution: Praising effort encourages a growth mindset: the belief that ability improves with work
questions.hint: Dweck contrasted a fixed mindset with another one

questions.text: Jack touches a hot pan. Which type of neuron carries the message from his skin to his spinal cord? Give the type.

feedback.motor neuron: Motor neurons carry messages FROM the CNS to muscles
feedback.motor: Motor neurons carry messages FROM the CNS to muscles
feedback.relay neuron: Relay neurons work inside the CNS, linking sensory and motor neurons
feedback.relay: Relay neurons work inside the CNS, linking sensory and motor neurons

questions.solution: Sensory neurons carry messages from receptors (here, in the skin) to the central nervous system
questions.hint: The message starts at a receptor in the skin

questions.text: In McGarrigle and Donaldson's 'Naughty Teddy' study, more young children conserved number when a teddy 'accidentally' messed up the counters than when an adult moved them on purpose. What does this suggest?

options: Piaget's stages happen in a random order
Young children can never conserve number
Piaget may have underestimated what young children can do
feedback: Many young children DID conserve in the teddy version

questions.solution: When the change seemed accidental, more children conserved, suggesting Piaget's method made the task harder than it needed to be
questions.hint: Compare how many children conserved in each version of the task

questions.text: Hughes's policeman doll study found that most children aged 3½ to 5 could hide a doll so that two policemen could not see it. Which part of Piaget's theory does this challenge?

options: That conservation develops in the concrete operational stage

questions.solution: Hiding the doll means taking the policemen's point of view, so the study challenges Piaget's claim that pre-operational children are egocentric
questions.hint: To hide the doll, the child must imagine what the policemen can see

questions.text: In Tulving's 'gold' memory study, scans showed more activity at the front of the brain when participants thought about personal events, and more towards the back when they thought about facts. What does this suggest?

options: Episodic and semantic memories use exactly the same brain areas
Episodic and semantic memories are linked to different brain areas
Personal events are stored mainly at the back of the brain
Memory is not linked to brain activity
feedback: Personal (episodic) memories were linked to more activity at the FRONT

questions.solution: Episodic memories were linked to more frontal activity and semantic memories to more activity towards the back, so the two types seem to involve different areas
questions.hint: Personal events are episodic; facts are semantic

questions.text: A brain scan shows strong activity in the temporal lobe while a person listens to music. Which function of the temporal lobe does this fit?

feedback: The somatosensory area is in the parietal lobe
The motor area is in the frontal lobe
The visual area is in the occipital lobe

questions.solution: The temporal lobe contains the auditory area, which processes sound
questions.hint: Listening to music involves which sense?

questions.text: Which scanning technique uses a radioactive tracer injected into the bloodstream to show which brain areas are most active? Give the abbreviation.

feedback.CT: CT scans use X-rays to show brain structure, not activity
feedback.CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to show brain structure, not activity
feedback.fMRI: fMRI shows activity through changes in blood oxygen — no tracer is injected
feedback.MRI: MRI uses magnets and radio waves — no tracer is injected

questions.solution: PET (positron emission tomography) tracks a radioactive tracer to show active brain areas
questions.hint: The first letter of this three-letter scan stands for 'positron'

questions.text: Describe how Piaget said a child's schemas develop. Refer to assimilation, accommodation and equilibrium.

rubric.model_answer: Piaget said children build schemas, which are mental structures of knowledge. When a child meets new information that fits an existing schema, they assimilate it, for example calling a new breed of dog a dog. When new information does not fit, the child feels disequilibrium and must accommodate, changing the schema or making a new one, for example creating a 'cat' schema. Once the new information fits, the child returns to equilibrium, a state of balance. This cycle makes schemas more complex over time.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: schemas are mental structures of knowledge
1 mark: assimilation = fitting new information into an existing schema
1 mark: accommodation = changing a schema or creating a new one
1 mark: equilibrium = balance when information fits; disequilibrium drives change
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Schemas change through assimilation (fit in), accommodation (change the schema) and equilibrium (balance restored)
questions.hint: Define a schema first, then explain each process with a simple example

questions.text: Which statement about Willingham's view of learning styles is accurate?

options: He argued every student should be taught only in their preferred learning style
He argued kinaesthetic learners cannot learn from reading
He argued learning styles are controlled by the brainstem
He argued there is little evidence that teaching to a student's preferred learning style improves learning

questions.solution: Willingham argued that matching teaching to a preferred style (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic) is not supported by evidence; content should decide the method
questions.hint: Willingham was a critic of the learning styles idea

questions.text: Which statement about the James-Lange theory of emotion is accurate?

options: Physical changes in the body happen first, and the emotion comes from noticing them
The emotion is felt first and then causes physical changes
Emotions are produced only by the cerebellum
Emotions are learned only by copying others
feedback: That is the common-sense view that the James-Lange theory argued against

questions.solution: James-Lange: an event causes physical arousal, and we then experience the emotion ('we are afraid because we tremble')
questions.hint: In this theory, which comes first: the body's reaction or the feeling?

questions.text: Which statement fits Hebb's theory of learning?

options: The number of connections between neurons is fixed, so learning cannot change the brain
Repeated activity strengthens the connections between neurons, forming cell assemblies
Learning happens only in the sensorimotor stage
Neurotransmitters stop working once something has been learned

questions.solution: Hebb said learning strengthens connections between neurons that fire together, forming cell assemblies: the brain is 'plastic'
questions.hint: Hebb believed the brain changes physically when we learn

questions.text: Which finding supports the role of nurture (the environment) in brain development?

options: The brainstem develops before the cortex in healthy foetuses
Identical twins share all of their genes
Rats raised in cages with toys and other rats developed a thicker cortex than rats raised alone
Babies are born with a sucking reflex
feedback: A fixed order of development in every foetus points to nature
A reflex present at birth points to nature

questions.solution: An enriched environment changed the rats' brains, so experience (nurture) affects brain development
questions.hint: Look for the finding where the environment was changed

questions.text: A child can solve problems about real, physical objects but cannot yet reason about abstract or hypothetical ideas. According to Piaget, which stage is the child in? Give the stage name.

feedback.formal operational: Formal operational thinkers CAN reason about abstract ideas
feedback.formal operational stage: Formal operational thinkers CAN reason about abstract ideas
feedback.formal: Formal operational thinkers CAN reason about abstract ideas

questions.solution: The concrete operational stage (7–11): logical thinking about real objects, but not yet abstract reasoning
questions.hint: Abstract reasoning develops in the final stage, so think about the stage before it

questions.text: Evaluate Piaget's theory of cognitive development.

rubric.model_answer: A strength is that Piaget's theory has been very influential in education: it led to child-centred, discovery learning and the idea of readiness. His tasks, such as conservation tasks, showed clear age differences. However, Piaget may have underestimated young children. McGarrigle and Donaldson found more children conserved when a 'naughty teddy' changed the counters, and Hughes found most young children could hide a doll from policemen, challenging egocentrism. Piaget also used small samples, including his own children, so results may not generalise.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a relevant strength identified (e.g. influence on education)
1 mark: the strength explained or supported
1 mark: a relevant weakness identified (e.g. underestimates children)
1 mark: supporting evidence named (e.g. McGarrigle and Donaldson, Hughes)
1 mark: a second weakness (e.g. small or biased samples, task wording)
1 mark: a balanced conclusion
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Strengths: influence on education, clear age-related findings. Weaknesses: underestimates children (Naughty Teddy, policeman doll), small samples
questions.hint: Give at least one strength and two weaknesses, each backed by evidence

questions.text: What is the term for changing your behaviour or opinions to fit in with a group? Give the term.

feedback.obedience: Obedience is following a direct order from an authority figure — this is about fitting in with a group

questions.solution: Conformity is going along with the majority, either to fit in or because you think the group is right
questions.hint: Asch studied this with a line-judging task

questions.text: What is the term for following a direct order from a person in authority? Give the term.

feedback.conformity: Conformity is going along with a group — here there is a direct order from an authority figure

questions.solution: Obedience is doing what an authority figure tells you to do; Milgram studied it
questions.hint: Milgram studied this with a fake shock machine

questions.text: In Milgram's 1963 study, who did the real participants believe they were giving electric shocks to?

options: A 'learner' who was actually a confederate working with Milgram
Another real participant chosen at random

questions.solution: The 'learner' was a confederate (an actor); no real shocks were given, but participants believed they were real
questions.hint: The learner was not really a participant at all

questions.text: What task did participants do in Asch's conformity study?

options: Estimate how many beans were in a jar
Judge which of three lines matched a standard line in length
Give electric shocks to a learner
feedback: Estimating the number of beans in a jar was Jenness's study
That was Milgram's obedience study

questions.solution: Asch's participants judged line lengths after hearing confederates give wrong answers on critical trials
questions.hint: The correct answer was obvious when people did the task alone

questions.text: What is the term for losing your sense of personal identity when you are part of a crowd, often because you feel anonymous? Give the term.
questions.solution: Deindividuation: in a crowd, people can feel anonymous and less personally responsible, so they may act in ways they normally would not
questions.hint: Think about losing your individual identity

questions.text: What is the 'bystander effect'?

options: People are more likely to intervene in an emergency when other people are present
People always obey a person in uniform
People are less likely to intervene in an emergency when other people are present
People change their answers to match a group

questions.solution: The bystander effect: the more bystanders there are, the less likely any one of them is to intervene
questions.hint: Think about what happens to each person's sense of responsibility in a crowd

questions.text: Roughly what proportion of participants in Asch's study conformed at least once on the critical trials?

feedback: About a third of all critical-trial ANSWERS conformed — but more participants than that conformed at least once
About a quarter of participants never conformed

questions.solution: About 75% conformed at least once; about a third of all answers on critical trials conformed; about 25% never conformed
questions.hint: Remember that about a quarter of participants never conformed

questions.text: In Milgram's original study, what percentage of participants went all the way to the highest shock level (450 volts)?

feedback: All participants went to at least 300 volts, but not all went to 450 volts

questions.solution: 65% (26 of 40) went to 450 volts, and all 40 went to at least 300 volts
questions.hint: It was much higher than experts predicted: almost two thirds

questions.text: Which is a dispositional factor affecting obedience?

options: The authority figure wearing a uniform
How close the authority figure is
feedback: Uniform is a situational factor
Location is a situational factor
Proximity is a situational factor

questions.solution: Dispositional factors are about the person (personality); situational factors are about the setting, such as uniform, location and proximity
questions.hint: Dispositional factors are inside the person rather than in the setting

questions.text: In Piliavin's New York subway study, which 'victim' was assisted more often?

options: The victim who carried a cane

questions.solution: The cane (ill) victim was assisted on almost every trial; the 'drunk' victim was assisted on about half of trials
questions.hint: Think about who passengers might see as deserving or as less costly to approach

questions.text: Bickman's study of the power of a uniform found that people were most likely to obey a stranger dressed as what?
questions.solution: Bickman found people obeyed the person dressed as a guard most, because the uniform signals authority
questions.hint: Which uniform suggests the most authority?

questions.text: In agency theory, what is the name for the state in which a person acts on behalf of an authority figure and does not feel responsible for their actions? Give the term.

feedback.autonomous state: In the autonomous state people act on their own free will and feel responsible
feedback.autonomous: In the autonomous state people act on their own free will and feel responsible

questions.solution: In the agentic state, people see themselves as agents carrying out someone else's wishes, so they feel less responsible (Milgram)
questions.hint: The person becomes an 'agent' of the authority figure

questions.text: What term describes the idea that when many people are present, each person feels less responsible for acting? Give the term.
questions.solution: Diffusion of responsibility: responsibility is spread across everyone present, so each person feels less need to act
questions.hint: The responsibility is 'spread out' among the people present

questions.text: Grace is sure the answer to a quiz question is 'Paris', but everyone else in her group says 'Rome'. She says 'Rome' too, even though she still thinks it is Paris. What is this an example of?

options: Normative social influence (wanting to fit in)
Informational social influence (wanting to be right)
feedback: Informational influence happens when you think the group knows better — Grace still thinks she is right

questions.solution: She goes along with the group publicly but does not change her private view, because she wants to fit in: normative influence
questions.hint: Has Grace changed her mind, or only what she says?

questions.text: A security guard tells shoppers to move away from a door, and they do. A man in casual clothes gives the same order and most people ignore him. Which factor affecting obedience does this show?
questions.solution: The uniform signals legitimate authority, so people are more likely to obey (as Bickman found)
questions.hint: What is different about the two people giving the order?

questions.text: At a football match, fans in masks and face paint, who feel they cannot be identified, shout insults they would never say on their own. Which concept explains this?

feedback: Nobody in authority gave them an order

questions.solution: Anonymity in a crowd reduces self-awareness and personal responsibility: deindividuation
questions.hint: The key clue is that the fans feel they cannot be identified

questions.text: In a variation of Asch's study, one confederate gave the correct answer. What happened to conformity?
questions.solution: When one other person disagreed with the majority, conformity dropped sharply: the group was no longer unanimous
questions.hint: Think about how much easier it is to disagree when someone else does too

questions.text: What term describes authority that is seen as having the right to give orders, such as a teacher in a school or a police officer? Give the two-word term.
questions.solution: Legitimate authority: people are more likely to obey someone they believe has the right to give orders
questions.hint: The first word means 'lawful' or 'proper'

questions.text: Ben sees a stranger drop their shopping in a busy street. He walks on, thinking someone else will pick it up. What is the name for this effect? Give the term.
questions.solution: The bystander effect (caused by diffusion of responsibility): with others around, Ben feels less personally responsible
questions.hint: There are lots of other people around who could step in

questions.text: In a study, participants were in a group with 1, 2, 3 or 6 confederates who all gave the same wrong answer. Conformity was 3% with 1 confederate, 13% with 2, 32% with 3 and 33% with 6. What do these results show?

options: Conformity rose as the group grew to 3, then levelled off
Conformity kept rising steadily as the group grew
Group size had no effect on conformity
Conformity was highest with one confederate
feedback: Going from 3 to 6 confederates only raised conformity from 32% to 33%

questions.solution: Conformity rose from 3% to 32% as the group grew to 3, but adding more people (33% with 6) made little difference
questions.hint: Compare the change from 1 to 3 with the change from 3 to 6

questions.text: In variations of a Milgram-style study, full obedience was 65% at a university, 48% in a run-down office building, 40% when the teacher and learner were in the same room, and 30% when the teacher had to hold the learner's hand on a shock plate. Which conclusion is supported?

options: Obedience rose when the study moved to an office building
Obedience fell as the teacher got physically closer to the learner
Location had no effect on obedience
Obedience was highest with the closest contact
feedback: Obedience fell from 65% to 48% in the office building
Obedience changed from 65% to 48% when the location changed

questions.solution: Obedience dropped from 40% (same room) to 30% (physical contact): closer proximity to the learner reduced obedience. The less prestigious location also lowered it (65% to 48%)
questions.hint: Compare the same-room and hand-on-plate figures

questions.text: Piliavin found no diffusion of responsibility on the subway: larger groups of passengers did not intervene less. Which explanation fits this finding?

options: Passengers were ordered by an authority figure to intervene
Passengers could clearly see the victim in a closed carriage, so it was hard to assume someone else would act
The victim was always a friend of the passengers

questions.solution: In a closed carriage the emergency was obvious and impossible to ignore, unlike studies where people could not see the victim
questions.hint: Think about how the subway carriage differs from hearing an emergency over an intercom

questions.text: Zimbardo found that participants wearing hoods and lab coats gave longer electric shocks than participants who wore name tags. What does this suggest?

options: Wearing any uniform always makes people kinder
People obey more when they can be identified
Name tags make people more aggressive
feedback: The participants with name tags gave SHORTER shocks

questions.solution: The hooded, anonymous participants were deindividuated and gave longer shocks: anonymity can increase antisocial behaviour
questions.hint: Which group could not be identified?

questions.text: In Milgram's study, the experimenter said phrases such as 'Please continue' and 'The experiment requires that you continue' when a participant hesitated. What were these phrases called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Milgram used four standard verbal prods, ending with 'You have no other choice, you must go on'
questions.hint: The experimenter used them to nudge or push participants to carry on

questions.text: Describe Asch's study of conformity.

rubric.model_answer: Asch tested male American students in groups. Only one person in each group was a real participant; the others were confederates. Each person said aloud which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. On critical trials, the confederates all gave the same wrong answer before the real participant answered. About a third of answers on critical trials conformed to the wrong majority, about 75% of participants conformed at least once and about 25% never conformed. In a control group, almost no mistakes were made.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: one real participant with a group of confederates
1 mark: the line-judging task, answers given aloud
1 mark: confederates gave the same wrong answer on critical trials
1 mark: a correct result (about a third of answers conformed, 75% at least once, or 25% never)
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: One real participant, confederates giving wrong answers on a line task; about a third of answers conformed, 75% conformed at least once
questions.hint: Describe who took part, what they did, and what was found

questions.text: Which is an ethical criticism of Milgram's study?

options: Participants were deceived about the true aim and were put under severe stress
Participants were not paid anything at all
The sample was made up of children
Participants were not allowed to give any shocks
feedback: Participants were paid for taking part
The participants were men aged 20–50

questions.solution: Participants were told it was a study of learning and many showed extreme stress; they were debriefed afterwards
questions.hint: Think about what participants were told and how they felt during the study

questions.text: Which statement about Asch's study is accurate?

options: Every participant conformed on every critical trial
About a quarter of participants never conformed on any critical trial
Conformity rose when one confederate gave the right answer
The task was so hard that people usually got it wrong when alone
feedback: A supporter who broke the majority made conformity FALL
Alone, people almost never made mistakes

questions.solution: About 25% of participants never conformed; alone (in the control condition), people almost never made mistakes
questions.hint: Remember the overall pattern: many conformed at least once, but not everyone

questions.text: Which is a limitation of Asch's study when applying its findings to other people?

options: There was no control group to compare with
It took place in a natural setting with no controls
All participants were American male students, so the results may not apply to women or other cultures
Participants were told the true aim at the start
feedback: Asch did use a control group, who answered alone
It was a laboratory study
Participants were deceived about the aim

questions.solution: The sample was American male students, so the findings may not generalise to other groups or cultures
questions.hint: Think about who the participants were

questions.text: Which statement about situational and dispositional explanations of obedience is accurate?

options: Dispositional explanations focus on uniform and location
Situational explanations say only personality matters
Both explanations ignore the role of authority figures
Situational ones focus on the setting (e.g. uniform, location); dispositional ones focus on personality

questions.solution: Situational = features of the setting (uniform, location, proximity); dispositional = features of the person (e.g. authoritarian personality)
questions.hint: 'Situation' means the setting; 'disposition' means personality

questions.text: Milgram said people can shift from acting on their own free will to acting for an authority figure. What is the name of the state in which people act on their own free will and feel responsible for their actions? Give the term.

feedback.agentic state: In the agentic state people act for the authority figure and feel LESS responsible
feedback.agentic: In the agentic state people act for the authority figure and feel LESS responsible

questions.solution: In the autonomous state people feel responsible for their own actions; in the agentic state they act for the authority figure
questions.hint: It is the opposite of the agentic state

questions.text: Explain how situational factors can affect obedience. Use evidence in your answer.

rubric.model_answer: Situational factors are features of the setting. Proximity matters: in Milgram's variations, obedience fell when the teacher was in the same room as the learner and fell further when they had to touch the learner. Location matters: obedience was lower in a run-down office than at a prestigious university, as the authority seemed less legitimate. Uniform matters: Bickman found people were more likely to obey a stranger dressed as a guard than one in everyday clothes, because a uniform signals authority.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: situational factors defined (features of the setting)
1 mark: proximity explained
1 mark: evidence for proximity (Milgram variation)
1 mark: location or uniform explained
1 mark: evidence (Milgram's office building or Bickman's guard)
1 mark: clear link to legitimacy of authority
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Proximity, location and uniform all change obedience: Milgram's variations and Bickman's guard uniform study
questions.hint: Choose two or three factors and back each one with a study

questions.text: In an experiment, what is the name of the variable that the researcher changes or manipulates? Give the term.

feedback.dependent variable: The dependent variable is the one that is MEASURED
feedback.DV: The dependent variable is the one that is MEASURED

questions.solution: The independent variable (IV) is changed by the researcher; the dependent variable (DV) is measured
questions.hint: It is the cause the researcher sets up, not the outcome

questions.text: In an experiment, what is the name of the variable that is measured? Give the term.

feedback.independent variable: The independent variable is the one the researcher CHANGES
feedback.IV: The independent variable is the one the researcher CHANGES

questions.solution: The dependent variable (DV) is measured to see whether it has been affected by the independent variable
questions.hint: Its value 'depends' on the change the researcher makes

questions.text: What is a hypothesis?

options: A testable prediction about what will happen in a study
A summary of the results after a study
A list of the participants in a study
A question asked in an interview

questions.solution: A hypothesis is a clear, testable statement predicting the outcome of a study
questions.hint: It is written before the study starts

questions.text: Which sampling method uses a method such as picking names out of a hat, so that every member of the target population has an equal chance of being chosen?

feedback: Systematic sampling picks every nth person from a list

questions.solution: Random sampling gives everyone in the target population an equal chance of selection, for example by drawing names
questions.hint: Picking from a hat is down to chance

questions.text: Which ethical guideline means participants must be told that they can leave a study at any time? Give the term.
questions.solution: The right to withdraw: participants can leave at any point and can ask for their data to be removed
questions.hint: Participants have the 'right' to do something

questions.text: What does 'debriefing' mean in research?

options: Asking participants to agree to take part before the study starts
Telling participants the true aim of the study and answering their questions at the end
feedback: That is informed consent
That is confidentiality

questions.solution: Debriefing happens at the end: participants are told the real aim and any deception is explained
questions.hint: It happens after the study is finished

questions.text: Which experimental design uses the SAME participants in every condition?

feedback: Independent groups uses different participants in each condition
Matched pairs uses different but matched participants in each condition

questions.solution: In repeated measures, every participant does every condition, so participant variables are controlled but order effects can occur
questions.hint: Each participant does the task more than once

questions.text: What is a confounding variable?

options: A variable other than the IV that has affected the results
The variable that the researcher changes
The variable that the researcher measures
feedback: That is the independent variable
That is the dependent variable

questions.solution: A confounding variable is an extra variable that has changed the DV, so we cannot be sure the IV caused the result
questions.hint: It 'confuses' the results

questions.text: Which of these is an example of qualitative data?

options: A participant's description of how they felt during a task
A score out of 20 on a test

questions.solution: Qualitative data is in words (descriptions, feelings); quantitative data is in numbers
questions.hint: Qualitative data is not in numbers

questions.text: Which type of experiment takes place in a controlled, artificial environment, where the researcher manipulates the IV?

feedback: A field experiment takes place in a natural, everyday setting
In a natural experiment the IV changes naturally; the researcher does not manipulate it

questions.solution: A laboratory experiment has high control in an artificial setting; a field experiment manipulates the IV in a natural setting
questions.hint: Think about where the most control is possible

questions.text: Which sampling method selects people who happen to be available at the time, such as students in a school canteen? Give the term.
questions.solution: Opportunity sampling uses whoever is available and willing at the time; it is quick but may be biased
questions.hint: The researcher takes the chance to use whoever is there

questions.text: What name is given to a small trial run of a study, carried out before the main study to find problems? Give the term.
questions.solution: A pilot study tests the procedure on a few participants so that problems can be fixed before the main study
questions.hint: It is like a practice run before the real thing

questions.text: A researcher tests whether music affects concentration. Participants complete a puzzle with music and without music, and their puzzle scores are recorded. What is the independent variable?

options: Whether music is played or not
feedback: The puzzle score is what is measured, so it is the dependent variable

questions.solution: The IV is what the researcher changes: music or no music. The puzzle score is the DV
questions.hint: What does the researcher change between the two conditions?

questions.text: A psychologist investigates whether sleep affects memory. One group sleeps 8 hours and another group sleeps 4 hours; then both groups take a memory test. What is the dependent variable?

options: The scores on the memory test
The number of hours of sleep
Which group each participant is in
The type of memory test chosen
feedback: Hours of sleep is what the psychologist changes, so it is the IV

questions.solution: The DV is what is measured: memory test scores. The IV is the hours of sleep
questions.hint: What is measured at the end?

questions.text: Participants take a memory test in the morning and the same type of test again in the evening. Some do better in the evening simply because they have had practice. What is this problem called?
questions.solution: Practice (or fatigue) from doing one condition first is an order effect, a problem in repeated measures designs
questions.hint: The problem comes from the order in which the conditions were done

questions.text: To reduce order effects in a repeated measures design, half the participants do condition 1 then condition 2, and the other half do condition 2 then condition 1. What is this technique called?
questions.solution: Counterbalancing balances out order effects across the two conditions
questions.hint: The two orders 'balance' each other out

questions.text: Hypothesis: 'Students who revise with music will recall fewer words than students who revise in silence.' This states the direction of the difference. What type of hypothesis is it? Give the term.

feedback.non-directional: A non-directional hypothesis predicts a difference without saying which way
feedback.non directional: A non-directional hypothesis predicts a difference without saying which way
feedback.two-tailed: A two-tailed hypothesis predicts a difference without saying which way
feedback.two tailed: A two-tailed hypothesis predicts a difference without saying which way
feedback.null: A null hypothesis predicts NO difference

questions.solution: It is directional (one-tailed) because it predicts which group will do better
questions.hint: Does it say which group will recall more?

questions.text: A researcher puts up a poster asking for people to take part in a study, and uses everyone who replies. Which sampling method is this? Give the term.
questions.solution: Volunteer (self-selected) sampling: participants choose to take part by replying to an advert
questions.hint: The participants put themselves forward

questions.text: In a study, the mean number of words recalled was 14 in the 'silence' condition and 9 in the 'music' condition. Which conclusion fits these results?

options: There was no difference between the conditions
Every participant recalled more words in silence
On average, participants recalled more words in silence than with music
feedback: A mean is an average — some individuals may have done better with music

questions.solution: The mean was higher in silence (14 vs 9), so on average recall was better in silence. A mean does not tell us about every individual
questions.hint: Compare the two means, and remember what a mean does and does not show

questions.text: A researcher watches children in a playground from a hidden position, so the children do not know they are being studied. What type of observation is this?

feedback: Overt means the participants know they are being observed
The researcher is not joining in with the children

questions.solution: Covert means hidden: the children do not know they are being observed, so they behave naturally
questions.hint: Do the children know they are being watched?

questions.text: Two observers watch the same video of children playing and both record the number of aggressive acts. Their tallies are very similar. What does this show?

options: The observation has good inter-observer reliability
The observation has good ecological validity
The study used a matched pairs design

questions.solution: When different observers record similar results, the observation has good inter-observer (inter-rater) reliability
questions.hint: Reliability is about consistency

questions.text: A study finds that as hours spent on social media go up, hours of sleep go down. What type of correlation is this?

feedback: In a positive correlation both variables increase together

questions.solution: As one variable increases the other decreases: a negative correlation
questions.hint: Do the two variables move in the same direction or opposite directions?

questions.text: A test gives similar scores when the same participants take it again a week later. Which quality of the test does this show? Give the term.

feedback.validity: Validity is whether a test measures what it claims to measure — consistency is a different quality
feedback.valid: Validity is whether a test measures what it claims to measure — consistency is a different quality

questions.solution: Getting consistent results when a test is repeated shows reliability (test-retest reliability)
questions.hint: This quality is about consistency

questions.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a laboratory experiment.

rubric.model_answer: Strength: the researcher has high control over extraneous variables, for example using the same room, instructions and timing for everyone. This makes it easier to show that the IV caused the change in the DV, and the study can be repeated to check reliability. Weakness: the setting is artificial, so people may not behave as they would in everyday life. This means the study may have low ecological validity, and participants may show demand characteristics because they know they are being studied.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: strength identified (e.g. high control, can be replicated)
1 mark: strength explained (e.g. cause and effect can be established)
1 mark: weakness identified (e.g. artificial setting)
1 mark: weakness explained (e.g. low ecological validity or demand characteristics)
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Strength: control of variables, so cause and effect can be shown. Weakness: artificial setting, so low ecological validity
questions.hint: Think about control (good) and how realistic the setting is (bad)

questions.text: A study finds a strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and the number of people swimming outdoors. Which conclusion is valid?

options: Eating ice cream causes people to go swimming
Swimming causes people to buy ice cream
There is no relationship between the variables
The two variables are related, but this does not show that one causes the other

questions.solution: Correlation does not show cause and effect; a third variable, such as hot weather, may affect both
questions.hint: Can a correlation tell us what causes what?

questions.text: Why might a researcher use a matched pairs design rather than an independent groups design?

options: To reduce the effect of participant variables between the conditions
So that each participant can do every condition
To make the study quicker to set up
feedback: Doing every condition describes repeated measures
Matching takes extra time to set up

questions.solution: Matching participants on key features (such as age or IQ) reduces participant variables while avoiding order effects
questions.hint: What is the risk when two different groups of people are compared?

questions.text: Which statement about ecological validity is accurate?

options: It is how consistent results are when a study is repeated
It is how far findings can be applied to real-life settings
It means the study was carried out outdoors
It is the number of participants in a study
feedback: Consistency when repeated is reliability

questions.solution: Ecological validity is how well findings generalise to everyday, real-life settings
questions.hint: 'Ecological' refers to the environment people normally live in

questions.text: Participants guess the aim of a study and change their behaviour to please the researcher. What is this called, and which procedure can reduce it?

options: Investigator effects — reduced by random sampling
Demand characteristics — reduced by a single-blind procedure
Social desirability — reduced by a pilot study
feedback: Counterbalancing reduces order effects, but the problem described is about guessing the aim

questions.solution: Demand characteristics are cues that reveal the aim; a single-blind procedure (participants don't know the aim or condition) reduces them
questions.hint: First name the problem, then think about what participants would need NOT to know

questions.text: A researcher knows which condition each participant is in and may treat them differently without realising. Which procedure, in which neither the participants nor the person running the study know the conditions, would reduce this? Give the term.

feedback.single-blind: In a single-blind procedure only the participants are unaware — here the researcher must be unaware too
feedback.single blind: In a single-blind procedure only the participants are unaware — here the researcher must be unaware too

questions.solution: A double-blind procedure reduces both investigator effects and demand characteristics
questions.hint: Two groups of people are kept unaware

questions.text: A psychologist wants to find out whether students recall more words when they revise in silence or with music. Describe how she could carry out an experiment to test this.

rubric.model_answer: Use an opportunity sample of 30 students from one school, randomly allocated to two conditions (independent groups) to avoid order effects. IV: silence or music. Each group studies the same list of 20 words for 2 minutes in the same room, with standardised instructions. Then each student writes down as many words as they can in 2 minutes. DV: number of words recalled. Compare the mean scores. Ethics: get informed consent, give the right to withdraw, keep data confidential and debrief at the end.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: suitable sample and sampling method
1 mark: experimental design with a reason (e.g. independent groups to avoid order effects)
1 mark: IV clearly operationalised
1 mark: DV clearly operationalised (number of words recalled)
1 mark: standardised procedure / controls
1 mark: an ethical issue and how it is dealt with
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Sample, design, IV (music vs silence), DV (words recalled), controls such as the same list and timing, and ethics
questions.hint: Plan the who, the conditions, what is measured, the controls and the ethics
